voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.
title: Laws of motion applications: from impulse to banked roads

chapters.title: Impulse changes momentum
chapters.formula: J = integral F dt = delta p; p = mv
points: Keep the signs of initial and final velocity.
Signed area under a force-time graph gives impulse.
System momentum is conserved when its net external impulse is zero.
chapters.script: Welcome back. We have learned to draw forces. Now let us use those diagrams to solve richer problems, without collecting a mountain of unrelated formulas. First, momentum. For a constant mass, momentum is mass times velocity. It is a vector, so direction matters. Impulse tells us how much momentum changes. For a constant force, impulse is force times the time interval. For a changing force, it is the signed area under the force versus time graph. Imagine a two kilogram ball moving right at three meters per second. After a hit, it moves left at two meters per second. Choose right as positive. What is its change in momentum? Take a moment. Initial momentum is plus six. Final momentum is minus four. Final minus initial gives minus ten kilogram meters per second, or minus ten newton seconds. If the hit lasts zero point two seconds, the average net force is minus fifty newtons. Subtracting speeds would miss the reversal. Now look at a triangular net force pulse. Its base is zero point four seconds and its peak is twenty newtons. The area is one half times base times height, or four newton seconds. For a half kilogram body, this gives an eight meter per second change in velocity. Finally, choose a whole system. Internal interaction forces cancel in its total momentum equation. When the net external impulse is zero, total momentum stays constant, although each object's momentum can change. A short collision may let us neglect a small external impulse, but we must state that approximation. In JEE, first decide which body or system your momentum equation describes.

chapters.title: Equilibrium means balancing components
points: Concurrent forces meet at one point in this particle model.
Resolve each tension along its own direction.
For a 100 N load and a 30 degree supporting rope: T = 200 N.
chapters.script: Let us pause the motion and study a knot in equilibrium. A light knot carries a downward load of one hundred newtons. One rope pulls it horizontally left. Another pulls up and right at thirty degrees above the horizontal. The ropes are taut, and we treat the knot as a particle with negligible mass. Which rope supports the vertical load? Picture the arrows before answering. Only the inclined rope has an upward component. Call its tension T. Its upward component is T sine thirty degrees, and its rightward component is T cosine thirty degrees. Vertical equilibrium says T sine thirty equals one hundred. Sine thirty is one half, so T is two hundred newtons. The horizontal rope must balance the rightward component. Its tension is two hundred times cosine thirty, or one hundred times the square root of three newtons, about one hundred seventy three point two. Notice something interesting. The inclined tension exceeds the weight. That is not a mistake: only part of this tension acts upward. Try changing the angle in your mind. A more nearly horizontal supporting rope needs a larger tension to provide the same vertical component. For concurrent forces on a particle, setting both component sums to zero gives equilibrium. For an extended rigid body, zero net force alone is not enough; torque must balance too. We study that in rotation. In an exam, mark whether an angle is measured from the horizontal or vertical. Swapping sine and cosine without checking the drawing is a very avoidable lost mark. Your diagram is doing the thinking before your calculator does the arithmetic.

chapters.title: Connected bodies share a constraint
chapters.formula: a = (m1 - m2)g / (m1 + m2); ideal Atwood machine
points: A light, inextensible, taut rope gives equal acceleration magnitudes.
A massless frictionless pulley and light rope give equal tensions.
3 kg and 2 kg with g = 10 m/s^2: a = 2 m/s^2; T = 24 N.
chapters.script: Here is an Atwood machine: two hanging masses connected by a rope over a pulley. Let the masses be three kilograms and two kilograms, and use g equal to ten meters per second squared. The rope is light, taut and inextensible. The pulley is massless and frictionless. These assumptions are part of the problem, not decorations. The rope constraint makes the acceleration magnitudes equal. One mass moves downward while the other moves upward. Our ideal pulley and rope also make the tension equal on both sides. Draw two separate free body diagrams. On the heavier mass, choose downward as positive: thirty minus T equals three a. On the lighter mass, choose upward as positive: T minus twenty equals two a. We have chosen different positive directions because the bodies move oppositely. Add the equations. Tension disappears, leaving ten equals five a. The acceleration is two meters per second squared. Now predict the tension. Is it automatically the weight of either mass? Think for a moment. No, because both masses accelerate. Substitute into the lighter mass equation: T minus twenty equals four. T is twenty four newtons. Check the heavier mass too: thirty minus twenty four equals six, which is three times two. Both diagrams agree. Adding equations is useful for finding acceleration; returning to one body gives tension. If the pulley has rotational inertia, its two tensions need not be equal. If a rope goes slack, the common acceleration constraint stops applying. JEE connected body problems become manageable when you separate actual forces from the geometric constraint connecting the bodies.

chapters.title: Choose the right friction model
chapters.formula: Static: |f| <= mu_s N; sliding: |f| = mu_k N
points: Check whether rest is possible before using limiting friction.
Normal force follows from the perpendicular force equation.
Rolling without slipping does not mean friction always equals mu_s N.
chapters.script: Friction deserves a decision, not just a substitution. Take a four kilogram block on a level floor, initially at rest. Use g equal to ten, a static coefficient of zero point five, and a kinetic coefficient of zero point three. With no other vertical forces, the normal reaction is forty newtons. The maximum static friction is twenty newtons. Apply an eighteen newton horizontal push. Does friction become twenty? Have a little think. No. It adjusts to eighteen newtons, opposing the tendency to slide, and the block remains at rest. Now apply twenty four newtons. Static friction cannot maintain rest. Once sliding begins, the kinetic friction magnitude is twelve newtons. The net horizontal force is twelve, so acceleration is three meters per second squared. The coefficient tells us a limit or a sliding model; it does not replace identifying the situation. What if the pull is angled upward? Its vertical component reduces the normal reaction while contact is maintained. Recalculate the normal force before calculating friction. On a stationary block on a simple incline, the required friction is m g sine theta and the normal reaction is m g cosine theta. Rest is possible when tangent theta is no greater than the static coefficient. Now distinguish sliding from rolling. In ideal pure rolling, the contact point does not slip relative to the surface. Static friction may act, but it is not automatically at its limiting value. A freely rolling wheel on an ideal horizontal surface can have zero friction. Real rolling resistance comes from effects such as deformation and is not generally the kinetic friction formula. For JEE, name the contact, find its slipping tendency, and only then choose the friction equation.

chapters.title: A level turn needs an inward force
chapters.formula: f = mv^2/r; v_max = sqrt(mu_s r g)
points: Centripetal force names the inward net force, not an extra interaction.
Static tire-road friction supplies the inward force in this ideal level-road model.
With mu_s = 0.5, r = 20 m, g = 10: v_max = 10 m/s.
chapters.script: A car turns left on a level road at constant speed. Is its acceleration zero? Its speed stays constant, but its velocity direction changes. It needs an inward acceleration of v squared divided by r. Now ask which real force supplies that acceleration. In a simplified level road model, static friction between the tires and road supplies the horizontal inward force. Weight and the normal reaction balance vertically. There is no separate force to add called centripetal force. That phrase describes the job done by the inward net force. With no other vertical forces, N equals m g. The required friction is m v squared over r. Its available maximum is mu s times m g. The no skid condition is therefore m v squared over r no greater than mu s m g. Mass cancels, giving a maximum speed equal to the square root of mu s r g. Try our example: coefficient zero point five, turn radius twenty meters, and g equal to ten. Under the square root we have one hundred. The maximum speed is ten meters per second. At six meters per second, is friction already at its maximum? Pause. No. For a one thousand kilogram car it is one thousand times thirty six divided by twenty, or eighteen hundred newtons, below the five thousand newton limit. For this calculation we neglect air forces, road irregularities and vehicle details. It is a physics model, not driving advice. Smaller radius means a tighter turn and a lower limiting speed. When you see a circular motion question, draw the actual forces first and write their inward components equal to m v squared over r.

chapters.title: Banking redirects the normal reaction
points: The bank rises outward; the normal reaction points upward and inward.
N cos(theta) = mg; N sin(theta) = mv^2/r without friction.
Below the ideal speed friction acts up the bank; above it, down the bank.
chapters.script: A banked road tilts upward toward the outside of a turn. This tilts the normal reaction inward, so part of that force can turn the car even without friction. Draw a cross section: inward is horizontal toward the center, while weight remains vertically downward. Let theta be the road's angle above horizontal. The normal reaction makes the same angle with the vertical. In the ideal frictionless model, its vertical component is N cosine theta. That balances m g because the car has no vertical acceleration. Its inward component is N sine theta. That equals m v squared over r. Divide the inward equation by the vertical equation. Both N and mass disappear. Tangent theta equals v squared divided by r g. So the ideal speed is the square root of r g tangent theta. Take a twenty meter radius, a forty five degree bank and g equal to ten. Tangent forty five equals one, giving ten times the square root of two meters per second, about fourteen point one four. This is the speed requiring no friction in our model, not a universal maximum. What happens below that speed? Think about a nearly stationary car on the slope. It tends to slide down the bank, so static friction acts up the bank. Above the ideal speed, the tendency reverses and friction acts down the bank. Resolve its vertical and inward components as well as the normal reaction. Do not assume N equals m g on a bank or insert mu N before checking whether friction is limiting. Wider speed range problems need those full component equations. Our toolkit now connects impulse, equilibrium, constraints and curved motion. Try the original practice questions next; they are JEE style, not claimed past paper questions.

quiz.question: A 2 kg ball changes velocity from +3 to -2 m/s in 0.2 s. Its average net force is:
quiz.explanation: Change in momentum = 2(-2 - 3) = -10 N s. Divide by 0.2 s to obtain -50 N.

quiz.question: A triangular positive net force pulse has base 0.4 s and height 20 N. For a 0.5 kg body, the change in velocity is:
A light knot supports a downward 100 N load with one horizontal rope and another at 30 degrees above horizontal. The inclined tension is:
quiz.explanation: Only the inclined rope supports the vertical load: T sin(30 degrees) = 100 N, so T = 200 N.

quiz.question: Ideal Atwood masses are 3 kg and 2 kg; g = 10 m/s^2. The rope tension is:
quiz.explanation: a = (3 - 2)10/(3 + 2) = 2 m/s^2. For the rising 2 kg mass, T - 20 = 2(2), so T = 24 N.

quiz.question: A 4 kg block initially rests on a level floor: mu_s = 0.5, mu_k = 0.3, g = 10 m/s^2. A horizontal 18 N push produces friction of:
quiz.explanation: The required 18 N is below the 20 N static limit. Static friction adjusts to 18 N and the block remains at rest.

quiz.question: For the same initially stationary block, a sustained 24 N horizontal push causes sliding. Its acceleration while sliding is:
quiz.explanation: 24 N exceeds the 20 N static limit. Sliding friction is 0.3(40) = 12 N, giving a = (24 - 12)/4 = 3 m/s^2.

quiz.question: In the ideal level-road model, mu_s = 0.5, r = 20 m and g = 10 m/s^2. The maximum no-skid speed is:
quiz.explanation: v_max = sqrt(mu_s r g) = sqrt(0.5 x 20 x 10) = 10 m/s.

quiz.question: A 45 degree bank has r = 20 m and g = 10 m/s^2. The speed requiring no friction is:
quiz.explanation: v = sqrt(r g tan(theta)) = sqrt(20 x 10 x 1) = 10 sqrt(2) m/s. This is the ideal speed, not a universal maximum.
